svg.title: Power distribution and injection: fanning one 5 V supply out to several runs
svg.desc: One 5 V supply feeds a main fuse, then a pair of distribution bus bars. Each run takes one fused red branch off the plus bus, and that single fuse feeds two red legs: one to the run's DI end and one to its far end. Each run likewise returns on two black legs, one from each end, to the minus bus. Data and its ground arrive separately from the Fadecandy, at the DI end only. Alongside: current per run, supply headroom, conductor ampacity and fuse sizing, running cost, and the choice between feeding both ends at full brightness and feeding the DI end alone under a brightness cap.
svg.text: Diagram 4 - Power distribution, conductor sizing, fusing and injection
Every number is worked from stated assumptions, so you can redo it for whatever layout you actually build.

Branch fuse: 6 A, one per run
1.25 × 3.84 = 4.8 A, and 6 A is the
smallest standard rating at or above it.
ONE fuse feeds BOTH of that run's red legs.
Branch wire: 14 AWG to 1.87 m
per leg - 0.150 V at 3.84 A. Size each
leg for the WHOLE 3.84 A, not half.
Fuses protect wire, not LEDs.
A 60 A supply will happily push 60 A
into a shorted 14 AWG branch. The fuse
is what stops that becoming a fire.
Fuse = smallest standard ≥ 1.25 × load
3 runs → 15 A, 6 runs → 30 A, 8 runs → 40 A.
Then ampacity ≥ the FUSE. One per feeder.
Order of assembly, every time
1. Supply off and unplugged.
2. Bus bars and main fuse.
3. Branch fuses.
4. Option A: far-end legs
soldered, sleeves resealed.
5. Ground first on every run,
then +5 V, then data.
6. Meter checks - see the
pre-power-on checklist.
7. Energise with ONE run
connected, then add the
rest one at a time.
0.50 V total, terminals to dimmest LED:
feeder .075 + bus .025 + branch .150,
then .250 inside the strip itself.
Sizing it for your own layout
1. Current per run - state the assumptions
64 px × 3 channels × 20 mA = 3.84 A full white, worst case
64 px × 60 mA = 3.84 A the same number, per px
3.84 A × 5 V = 19.2 W per run
20 mA per colour channel is the standard WS2812B figure. It is a
ceiling, not a typical: a warm scene at a third brightness is nearer
1.2 A. Size supplies and fuses for the ceiling regardless.
2. Supply headroom - 80 % continuous ceiling
runs × 3.84 A = worst case. Supply ≥ that ÷ 0.8
6 runs 23.0 A → S-150-5 (30 A) at 77 % ceiling
8 runs 30.7 A → S-150-5 (30 A) at 102 % DO NOT
8 runs 30.7 A → S-300-5 (60 A) at 51 % good
12 runs 46.1 A → S-300-5 (60 A) at 77 % ceiling
Your 30 A unit cannot carry eight full-white runs. Put the eight-run
starter on the 60 A unit. 18 runs = 6 + 12, both at 77 %, none spare.
Never parallel two supplies’ V+ outputs. Tie grounds, not V+.
3. Feeder gauge, main fuse, and how far it reaches
runs load fuse feeder: gauge and max length
Ampacity NEC T.310.16 60 C. Loop R NEC Ch.9 T.8 stranded 75 C.
A fuse must never exceed the ampacity of the wire it alone protects.
4. What it costs to leave on
18 runs, full white 69.1 A × 5 V = 345 W never happens
18 runs, ambient 25 % ≈ 86 W realistic
86 W × 5 h/day × 30 days ≈ 13 kWh/month
5. What the injection choice does not change
Nothing here. Every gauge and fuse rating is sized for full
white, because a fuse has to hold when the software is wrong.
Option A and Option B differ only in the number of leads.
Every figure here is derived in § 6.2 from NEC Table 310.16 (ampacity), Chapter 9 Table 8 (resistance), 240.6(A) (standard fuse ratings)
and 210.19(A) Informational Note No. 4 (the 3 % branch / 5 % total drop guidance). Sizing is also a layout decision: putting the supply
beside the block it feeds - 0.3 m rather than 1 m - takes the eight-run feeder from 4 AWG to 8 AWG, about 40 % of the cross-section.
Does a 64-pixel run need injection at its far end?
Do not apply an "inject every 2 m" length rule here. That number is
written for 60 LEDs/m strips, and yours are 30 LEDs/m. Current sets
the drop, not length, and half the density is half the current.
V = I_span × r_rail × L_span r_rail = Ω/m of ONE rail
A run fed from one end carries everything at the feed and nothing
at the tip, so the average is half - but both rails drop, and the
two cancel. Compare in amp-metres, not metres:
2.0 m of 60 LEDs/m 120 px 7.20 A × 2.00 m = 14.4 A·m the rule’s case
your run, 30 LEDs/m 64 px 3.84 A × 2.11 m = 8.10 A·m 56 % of it
That kills the 2 m rule - but it does not license a one-end feed
at full white.
The pads see 4.75 V, not 5.00 V: § 6.2 spends 0.25 V
getting there, so the strip’s own rails have 0.250 V.
Working from 5.00 V doubles every threshold at right.
1. How many points you feed the run at
points spans drop r_rail for 0.250 V
No flexible PCB strip reaches 0.031 Ω/m.
At full white a run is fed at BOTH ends. Fed from the DI end
alone, a 25 % cap needs 0.123 Ω/m - the very same strip.
Unverified: r_rail for your silicone-sleeved strips is not known
and was not established here. Do not substitute a generic figure.
2. Then settle it with a meter, not by eye.
Meter the strip’s solder pads, then its dimmest point - the
MIDPOINT under Option A, the FAR TIP under Option B. Pads minus
that reading must be 0.250 V or less; an absolute 4.50 V would
pass a strip that fails later, once the whole zone is lit.
